title: Stage 9, Lesson 9: Lending to family - the rules that keep the relationship
subtitle: Money and affection are the two things most capable of damaging each other once they are mixed
openingQuestion: A relative asks to borrow a large sum, promising to "pay it back in a few months". Which principle limits the damage to the relationship if repayment does not go smoothly?
openingOptions: Never lend money to a relative under any circumstances whatsoever
Only lend an amount you could live with never getting back
Always lend the full amount asked for, to keep the peace
Only lend verbally, since writing it down destroys the trust
explanation: The practical principle: only lend what you could live with losing outright - because the possibility of not being repaid (or of having to choose between chasing the debt and keeping the relationship) is real. Writing it down, even as a message confirming the amount, the date and the expected repayment, is not distrust; it is how you avoid a misunderstanding, because memories of amounts and deadlines usually diverge between two people over time.

diagram.label: Decide the amount you could live with losing outright
Write down the amount, the date and the expected repayment
If it runs late there is a shared record to talk from, not two memories

realWorldExample.description: Many serious family rifts start with a loan nobody wrote down - not because the sum was large, but because the two sides expected different repayment terms, or even disagreed about whether it was a gift or a loan in the first place.

quiz.question: Why is "only lend what you could live with losing" more useful than trying to predict whether the borrower can repay?
options: Because relatives usually have no assets to offer as collateral
Because you cannot predict a relative's ability to repay
Because the interest rate on a loan to family is usually zero
Because the law does not protect loans between individuals
quiz.explanation: You cannot control the borrower's future circumstances - job loss, illness, an unexpected financial squeeze - but you have complete control over the amount you decide to lend. Setting the limit by what you could lose is more practical risk management than forecasting an uncertain future.

quiz.question: Why should writing down a family loan, even in a message, NOT be read as "distrust"?
options: Because you need documentation to file a personal income tax return
Because the bank requires proof of where the money came from
Because the two sides will remember the amount and the deadline differently
Because a court will only take the case with a notarised contract
quiz.explanation: The issue is not doubting the borrower's intentions - it is that human memory is imperfect. After a few months the two sides can genuinely recall different amounts or different deadlines. A written record is a tool for protecting THE RELATIONSHIP from an honest misunderstanding, not a tool for suspicion.

quiz.question: Which principle limits your risk when lending to a relative?
options: Lend at most 20% of your current net worth
Only lend if the borrower has a stable income
Only lend where there is clear collateral available
Only lend an amount you would be fine losing
quiz.explanation: You do not control the borrower's future circumstances, but you completely control the amount you hand over. That is the one variable in your hands.

quiz.question: What most commonly causes conflict over loans within a family?
options: The two sides remember the amount or the deadline differently
The borrower deliberately withholds payment while able to pay
The agreed interest is higher than what a bank would charge
The lender demands the money back before the promised date
quiz.explanation: Both sides are usually being honest, but their memories of the agreement differed from the very beginning. This is exactly why one simple confirming message is worth far more than the effort it costs.

quiz.question: When is saying plainly "consider this a gift" the better option than lending?
options: When the sum is small enough not to disturb your own financial plans
When you already know the chance of being repaid is very low
When the borrower has not given a specific repayment date up front
When you want to avoid drawing up any paperwork recording the loan
quiz.explanation: An unpaid loan quietly corrodes a relationship one meeting at a time. Calling it a gift from the start means both sides know where they stand, and nobody has to keep up the pretence of a repayment schedule that was never real.

keyTakeaways: Only lend a relative an amount you could accept never getting back
Writing down the amount and the deadline protects the relationship from misunderstanding; it is not a sign of distrust
You cannot control the borrower's future circumstances, but you can control how much risk you accept

practicePrompt.question: Your cousin asks to borrow 50 million with no clear repayment plan. You have 50 million saved, but it is part of your emergency fund. Which principle should decide how much you lend?
options: Lend the whole 50 million immediately, because turning down a relative is never the right thing to do in any situation
Only lend a relative what you could accept never getting back - which means not touching the emergency fund
Lend twice what was asked for, as a show of generosity that strengthens the family relationship
Refuse every request to borrow money from a relative in every situation, with no exceptions at all
practicePrompt.explanation: Only lend a relative what you could accept never getting back. Write down the amount and the deadline so the relationship is protected from a misunderstanding.

application.title: Decide the amount before you hear the reason
application.message: Set a figure in advance that you could give away with the relationship intact if it never came back. When the request arrives, the answer is that figure or nothing - not a number that climbs with how urgent the story sounds.
application.secondary: Write it down even when you have already treated it as a gift. The note is not for a lawsuit; it is so the two of you remember the same amount and the same date three years from now.

sections.text: Money and affection are the two things most capable of damaging each other once they are mixed - but a few simple principles cut that risk considerably.
Set the limit by what you can absorb, not by a forecast of repayment

You cannot control the borrower's future circumstances, but you have complete control over the amount you decide to lend - so only lend what you could accept never getting back. Writing it down clearly, even in a message, is not a sign of distrust; it protects both sides from an honest misunderstanding, because memories of the amount and the deadline usually drift apart over time.

items: Only lend a relative an amount you could accept never getting back
A clear record protects the relationship from misunderstanding; it is not a sign of distrust
You cannot control the borrower's future circumstances, but you can control how much risk you take on

sections.text: Three questions to ask yourself before agreeing

items: If this money never comes back, am I still financially fine? If the answer is no, the amount under consideration is too large.
If this money never comes back, do I still have a relationship with this person? If not, lower the amount until the answer becomes yes.
Does this person need a loan, or do they need a solution? If the root problem is spending above income, a loan only postpones it and usually makes it larger.

left.label: A loan
left.text: It carries an expectation of repayment, so it creates an obligation and an awkward moment when the date arrives. Write down the amount, the date and the expected repayment so both sides read it the same way.

right.label: A gift
right.text: There is no expectation of getting it back, so there is no obligation. For a modest sum and someone close, saying plainly that this is a gift rather than a loan usually keeps the relationship in far better shape.

sections.text: Most of the conflict does not come from someone deliberately refusing to pay. It comes from two people remembering differently. One remembers a loan due back within six months; the other remembers being helped out, repayable whenever they can. Both are being honest, but the expectations diverged at the very start and only surface once it is late.

sections.label: One message is enough
sections.text: Family loans do not need a contract. One message naming three things - the amount, the date it was transferred, and when it is expected back - with the borrower confirming it, is enough for both sides to remember the same thing. It takes a minute and belongs at the moment of the transfer, while both people are comfortable, rather than at the moment you have to chase it.

sections.label: When the date passes and nothing arrives
sections.text: Asking early and gently always beats waiting in silence and then erupting. A direct question about how things stand, with an offer to split the repayment into instalments, usually preserves both the money and the relationship far better than holding it in until you cannot any longer.

lines: Clear rules from the start protect the money and the affection alike.
This is not coldness - it is how a relationship stays healthy over the long run.
